title: Ability
whenToUse: To express physical or mental ability or capacity
formula: Subject + can/could/be able to + base verb
examples: She could swim when she was five.
They will be able to join us tomorrow.
commonMistakes: Using 'to' after can or could (e.g., I can to swim)
Using 'could' for a single completed action in the past instead of 'was/were able to' or 'managed to'

title: Advice
whenToUse: To give suggestions, recommendations, or opinions about what is the right thing to do
formula: Subject + should/ought to/had better + base verb
examples: You should see a doctor about that cough.
We ought to leave early to avoid traffic.
You had better finish your report tonight.
commonMistakes: Using 'should to' instead of 'should' + base verb
Forgetting that 'had better' is stronger than 'should' and often implies a warning

title: Obligation
whenToUse: To express duty, necessity, rules, or strong obligation
formula: Subject + must/have to/need to + base verb
examples: I must remember to call my mother.
Students have to wear a uniform.
You mustn't smoke in the building.
commonMistakes: Using 'mustn't' when you mean 'don't have to' (mustn't = prohibited; don't have to = not necessary)
Using 'must' for past obligation instead of 'had to'

title: Probability
whenToUse: To express how certain, likely, or possible something is
examples: It's cloudy; it might rain later.
He hasn't eaten all day; he must be hungry.
That can't be true; I saw him in London yesterday.
commonMistakes: Using 'mustn't' instead of 'can't' for negative logical deduction
Confusing 'may' or 'might' for possibility with 'can' for ability or general possibility
